intro: Trees Atlanta keeps a list of the city's biggest trees, and its champions turn up in odd places, beside the drive to a tennis centre, on the pavement outside the High Museum, leaning over the BeltLine path, in a private yard in Poncey-Highland. These eleven trees come from that list. The tallest, a tulip tree in Atlanta Memorial Park, was measured at 50.6 metres. The oldest by its own account is the Grandfather Beech in southwest Atlanta, which Atlanta Magazine dates to 1863. Most are free to see.
meta_description: Atlanta's champion trees, from a 50.6-metre tulip tree by a tennis centre to the Grandfather Beech and the ginkgo outside the High Museum.
question_meta: The oldest tree on Atlanta's list is the Grandfather Beech, dated to 1863 by Atlanta Magazine. An Oakland Cemetery magnolia dates from after the Civil War.
question_answer: The oldest tree on this Atlanta list is the Grandfather Beech at the Outdoor Activity Center in southwest Atlanta, which Atlanta Magazine dates to 1863, about 160 years ago, though it gives no basis for the year. Close behind is a southern magnolia in Oakland Cemetery that a Confederate soldier's brother planted after the Civil War, and which now holds up the soldier's leaning gravestone. Most of the city's other champion trees have never been dated.
question_context: Atlanta's big trees are measured far more often than they are dated. The Trees Atlanta champion program records girth, height and crown for the largest tree of each species in the city, and almost none of those records carries an age. What the city does have is old ground. Herbert Taylor and Daniel Johnson parks in Morningside hold a remnant of the hickory and beech forest that stood there when the Muscogee (Creek) ceded the land in the 1820s, with some trees put at 150 to 180 years old or more. Fernbank Forest in Druid Hills, 65 acres of old growth bought by local citizens in 1939, has tulip poplars and white oaks on one slope reaching about 156 feet. The Outdoor Activity Center in southwest Atlanta keeps another remnant, and the Grandfather Beech inside it, dated by Atlanta Magazine to 1863. In Oakland Cemetery, a magnolia planted after the Civil War grows against a soldier's grave. The tallest measured tree on this list, a tulip tree beside the Bitsy Grant Tennis Center, stands 50.6 metres and has no recorded age at all. If you know when any of these went in, tell us.

faq.q: Can you reach Atlanta's champion trees by MARTA?
faq.a: Some of them. The High Museum ginkgo is by the Woodruff Arts Center complex at Arts Center station, the Vine City elm is in the same neighbourhood as Vine City station, and King Memorial is the station closest to Oakland Cemetery. The trees in Herbert Taylor Park, Atlanta Memorial Park and Fernbank Forest are easier by car or bike.

faq.q: Do you need a ticket to see the trees?
faq.a: For nearly all of them, no. The parks, the BeltLine path along Tanyard Creek and the grounds of Oakland Cemetery are free, and the High Museum ginkgo stands by the public sidewalk, so no museum ticket is needed. Fernbank Forest is open daily until 4:30 pm; check with Fernbank Museum whether the forest needs a ticket. The Outdoor Activity Center lists no hours and closes on some Saturdays for events, so check before going.

faq.q: Can you visit the champion black tupelo in Poncey-Highland?
faq.a: Only from the street. It grows in a private yard at 622 Moreland Avenue NE and is clearly visible from the public sidewalk, which is where to stand. It is at its best in autumn colour.

trees.name: Herbert Taylor Park champion silver maple

location.address: Herbert Taylor Park, off Beech Valley Rd / Pasadena Ave NE (kiosk at 1343 Pasadena Ave NE)

trees.story:
Atlanta's champion silver maple grows on ground where amateur archaeologists have turned up Woodland pottery, made somewhere between 1000 BC and 900 AD. The tree is a newcomer by that measure, but a big one. Trees Atlanta's champion program ranks it first for its species in the city, with a trunk 417 centimetres round and a height of 31 metres. A measurer from the Eastern Native Tree Society recorded a silver maple in the same preserve in January 2012 at 376 centimetres round and about 34 metres tall. If that was this tree, the two counts disagree, and nobody has said which tape went round where.

Silver maples are floodplain trees, and this one has found the right address. Herbert Taylor Park and the neighbouring Daniel Johnson Park make 39 acres where Rock Creek meets the South Fork of Peachtree Creek, steep granite slopes that were once quarried above bottomlands farmed for centuries. The Old-Growth Forest Network counts the woods as a remnant of the hickory and beech forest that stood here when the Muscogee (Creek) ceded the land in the 1820s, with some trees put at 150 to 180 years old or more. Trillium and sweet cicely carpet the ground.

The park's Friends group counts more than a dozen city champions here, and a champion northern red oak stands about 90 metres away, so plan a walk rather than a single stop. Nobody has dated the maple itself. If you know its age, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size for a silver maple, a trunk about 417 centimetres round. It stands in the Herbert Taylor Park woods, about 90 metres from the park's champion northern red oak.

trees.name: Herbert Taylor Park champion northern red oak

location.address: Herbert Taylor Park, Morningside (about 90 m from atl_001)

trees.story:
This northern red oak joined Atlanta's champion tree list in 2026 at 41.8 metres tall, and it still ranks only third for its species in the city. That says something about the oaks of this corner of Morningside. Trees Atlanta's champion program records a trunk 358 centimetres round on a tall, narrow-crowned forest oak, the kind that grows up rather than out. The figures come from the program's own record alone, so read them as one measurement until somebody repeats it. A nomination this year does at least settle one thing. The tree is alive.

It grows in the preserve formed by two gifts to the city. Daniel Johnson Park was deeded in 1935, and Herbert Taylor Park was handed over from 1972 onwards. Together they make 39 acres of steep slope and creek bottom where Rock Creek joins the South Fork of Peachtree Creek. The Old-Growth Forest Network lists the woods as a remnant of the hickory and beech forest that stood here when the Muscogee (Creek) ceded this land in the 1820s, and amateur archaeologists have found pottery from the Woodland period in the ground.

The oak is one of more than a dozen champions the park's Friends group counts here, and the city's champion silver maple stands about 90 metres away. Walk them together. Nobody has put an age on this oak. If you know more, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height, 41.8 metres on a narrow-crowned trunk 358 centimetres round. It stands in the Herbert Taylor Park woods, about 90 metres from the champion silver maple.

trees.name: Atlanta's tallest measured tree, Memorial Park tulip poplar

location.address: Atlanta Memorial Park, beside the entrance road to the Bitsy Grant Tennis Center, 2125 Northside Dr NW

trees.story:
At 50.6 metres, this tulip tree is the tallest on our Atlanta list, and one of the tallest trees in the city by the reckoning of the man who keeps its champion register. Eli Dickerson, the volunteer ecologist behind the list, measured it at 166 feet, nearly 17 storeys, and showed it off on a champion tree hike in October 2015 that went ahead in the rain. Trees Atlanta's program records 50.6 metres and a trunk 429 centimetres round, and still ranks it second among the city's tulip trees on points.

It does not stand anywhere grand. It towers alongside the road into the Bitsy Grant Tennis Center in Atlanta Memorial Park, where players pass it on the way to their courts. For scale, the tallest tulip poplars in Fernbank Forest across town are recorded at about 156 feet. This one clears them by ten.

The park keeps a memory of its own. In the 1930s, pupils from local schools planted trees here to honour figures from Atlanta's past, but nobody recorded which, and this tree cannot be tied to them. Nobody has dated it either.

The city's champion white oak stands a short way up the slope, so the two make one stop. The latest published sighting of the tulip tree is from 2015. If you have walked past it since, tell us it is still there.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height, 50.6 metres on a trunk 429 centimetres round. It stands alongside the road into the Bitsy Grant Tennis Center, with the champion white oak a short way up the slope.

trees.name: Memorial Park champion white oak

location.address: Atlanta Memorial Park, forest southwest of the Bitsy Grant Tennis Center, Northside Dr NW

trees.story:
The biggest white oak in Atlanta grows in the woods behind a public tennis centre. Trees Atlanta's champion program ranks it first for its species in the city, with a trunk 446 centimetres round and a height of 43.3 metres, and places it in the forest southwest of the Bitsy Grant Tennis Center in Atlanta Memorial Park. It was nominated in 2011.

When the volunteers who keep the list walked the park in the rain in October 2015, they stopped first at the champion tulip tree beside the tennis road, then climbed to what Rough Draft Atlanta described as a big white oak on a hill. The report gives no size, so it cannot be said for certain that the oak they visited was this champion, though the program puts its champion on that same slope.

The measurements come from one record, the program's own, so treat them as that measurer's figures. Its pin sits within about a metre of the tulip tree's, which means it marks the stand rather than the trunk. Start at the tulip tree by the road and look up the slope. In the 1930s, local schoolchildren planted trees in this park to honour figures from Atlanta's past; no source says which, and nothing ties this oak to them.

Nobody has dated it. If you know its age, or have seen it lately, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its trunk, 446 centimetres round, on an oak 43.3 metres tall. It stands in the woods up the slope southwest of the Bitsy Grant Tennis Center, above the champion tulip tree by the road.

trees.name: High Museum ginkgo

location.address: High Museum of Art, 1280 Peachtree St NE (street frontage)

trees.story:
The biggest ginkgo in Atlanta grows on the Peachtree Street frontage of the High Museum of Art, and you do not need a ticket to see it. Trees Atlanta's champion program ranks it first for its species, with a trunk 472 centimetres round, a height of 27.5 metres and a crown about 26 metres across, worth 297.7 points on the champion scale.

It has not had an easy life. Atlanta Magazine, profiling the city's champions in April 2025, wrote that nearby renovations, pollution and ordinary city life have stressed its health for decades. It is still standing. It lives beside one of the busiest roads in Atlanta, and the magazine counts it among the city's street survivors, champions that hold on where few trees would choose to grow.

Museumgoers and passers-by stop for it through the year, but mostly in autumn, when the magazine says its leaves turn a yellow worthy of Van Gogh. That is the time to come.

MARTA's Arts Center station sits beside the Woodruff Arts Center complex, so this is a champion you can reach by train. Nobody has published when it was planted. If you know, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its fan-shaped leaves and its trunk, 472 centimetres round. It stands by the public sidewalk on the Peachtree Street frontage of the High Museum of Art.

trees.name: Louise G. Howard Park champion white ash

location.address: Louise G. Howard Park, beside the paved path along Tanyard Creek (BeltLine path just north of Collier Rd)

trees.story:
This white ash is one of the few Atlanta champions that also holds the title for the whole of Georgia, and the people who look after it are not sure how long it has left. It has taken lightning strikes, and the emerald ash borer, an invasive beetle, has found it. In April 2025 Atlanta Magazine reported that arborists worry it may not be around much longer.

For now it is still enormous. Trees Atlanta's champion program records a trunk 436 centimetres round and a height of 40.6 metres. The magazine prints 129 feet, about 39 metres, so the two measurements differ by a metre and a half, and its crown spreads about 17 metres. It has been on the city's list since 2010.

You do not have to go looking for it. It leans over the paved path that runs beside Tanyard Creek in Louise G. Howard Park, on the stretch of BeltLine trail just north of Collier Road, so walkers, runners and cyclists pass beneath it all day. It is an easy champion to visit and a plainly troubled one, which is a reason to go sooner rather than later.

Nobody has published its age. If you know it, or if you pass the tree and see that it has changed, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the way it leans over the paved path beside Tanyard Creek, on a trunk 436 centimetres round. It stands on the BeltLine path in Louise G. Howard Park, just north of Collier Road.

trees.name: Grandfather Beech at the Outdoor Activity Center

location.address: West Atlanta Watershed Alliance Outdoor Activity Center, 1442 Richland Rd SW

trees.story:
Atlanta Magazine says the Grandfather Beech dates back to 1863, which would make it a seedling the summer before the Battle of Atlanta. The magazine does not say how it knows, so take the year as its claim, and roughly 160 years as the age that follows from it.

The size is not in doubt. Trees Atlanta's champion program records it at 36.7 metres tall, with a trunk 345 centimetres round and a crown about 27 metres across, third among the city's American beeches. It has a viewing platform and a bench of its own, so visitors can sit under the towering limbs and look at the smooth, silvery-grey bark.

It grows in the Outdoor Activity Center, a 26-acre nature preserve in southwest Atlanta that the magazine says holds one of the few old-growth forest remnants left in the city. The magazine suggests that growing among so many mature trees may be part of why the beech has lasted. The centre opened in 1975 as the Bush Mountain Outdoor Activity Center, on eight acres Atlanta Public Schools leased for a dollar a year, and in 2007 the National Wildlife Federation called it an ecological jewel. The West Atlanta Watershed Alliance runs it today under an agreement with the city.

The centre lists no opening hours and closes on some Saturdays for events, so check with it before you go.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the viewing platform and bench built beside it, and by its smooth, silvery-grey bark. It stands on the trails of the Outdoor Activity Center, 1442 Richland Road SW.

trees.name: Vine City champion American elm

location.address: Thurmond St NW at Magnolia St (641 Thurmond St NW), Vine City park

trees.story:
Atlanta's champion American elm is far wider than it is tall. Its crown spreads about 33 metres, while the tree itself reaches only 19.8 metres, and the trunk under all that shade is 381 centimetres round. Trees Atlanta's champion program ranks it first for its species in the city, on 242.5 points.

That it is here at all is the real surprise. Elms were once among the most common trees across the eastern United States, Atlanta Magazine noted in April 2025, until Dutch elm disease wiped out most of them in the middle of the twentieth century. This one came through. It sits on a gentle hill in Vine City, wide and low, and the magazine calls it a glorious specimen.

It came through a second test in 2017. When the park around it was being built, its champion status earned it protective treatment during the works, to make sure it was saved. The magazine counts it among the city's survivors, and it was still standing when that article went to print.

It joined the champion list in 2020. The Vine City MARTA station is in the same neighbourhood, and the park is free and open to walkers. Nobody has published when the elm was planted. If you know, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its shape, a crown about 33 metres across on a tree under 20 metres tall. It stands on a gentle hill in the park at Thurmond Street and Magnolia Street NW in Vine City.

trees.name: Fernbank Forest champion loblolly pine

location.address: Fernbank Forest, main path near Clifton Rd side, 767 Clifton Rd NE

trees.story:
Fernbank Museum says one of its champion loblolly pines is over 148 feet tall, about 45 metres. Which pine that is, the museum does not say. Atlanta's champion tree program measured this one, beside the main path near the Clifton Road side of Fernbank Forest, at 42.2 metres in 2010, on a trunk 280 centimetres round, and ranks it first for its species in the city. It may be the museum's 148-footer after fifteen more years of growth, or the honour may belong to another, because a second ranked loblolly stands nearby.

The forest is 65 acres of old growth in Druid Hills. Citizens bought it from Colonel Z. D. Harrison in 1939 and formed Fernbank, Inc. around it. White oaks and tulip poplars on one of its slopes reach about 156 feet, and a few loblollies match them.

The forest has been closed once in living memory. A lease dispute shut it in 2012, and it reopened in September 2016 after four years of restoration. It is now open daily for self-guided walks until 4:30 in the afternoon. The museum's page does not make clear whether a ticket is needed for the forest alone, so check before you go.

Nobody has dated this pine. If you know its age, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height, 42.2 metres when measured in 2010, on a trunk 280 centimetres round. It stands beside the main path in Fernbank Forest, near the Clifton Road side.

trees.name: Oakland Cemetery champion southern magnolia

location.address: Oakland Cemetery, near the Confederate Section, 248 Oakland Ave SE

trees.story:
In the Confederate Section of Oakland Cemetery, a soldier's gravestone leans against a southern magnolia his brother planted after the Civil War. The cemetery tells the story in its own history of its trees. Private Lucien Brahan Weakley is buried there, and the magnolia that grew from his brother's planting now holds up his stone. The cemetery's post puts that tree at 133 years old, but the post carries no date, so the count may be stale. Planted some time after 1865, it would be somewhere around 150 now.

Oakland is also home to Atlanta's champion southern magnolia, nominated in 2012 and ranked first in the city by the Trees Atlanta program, with a trunk 434 centimetres round, 19.9 metres tall and a crown about 20 metres across. Whether the champion and the Weakley magnolia are the same tree has not been settled. The program's record says only Oakland Cemetery, and no source puts its champion at Weakley's grave. Start at the leaning gravestone and you will have found at least one of them. If you can tell us whether it is the big one, please do.

The cemetery is on the National Register of Historic Places, and a 2016 tree walk there listed both the magnolia and a European cherry laurel among the city's champions. The grounds are free to enter. Tours are ticketed, but you do not need one for the trees.

trees.name: Poncey-Highland champion black tupelo

location.address: 622 Moreland Ave NE (view from the public sidewalk only)

trees.story:
The executive director of Trees Atlanta, Greg Levine, says he crazy loves this tree, and it grows in somebody's yard. It is a black tupelo in Poncey-Highland, flanked by houses, and it has been on the city's champion list since 2006.

By the standards of Atlanta's other champions it is not big. Trees Atlanta's program records a trunk 280 centimetres round and a height of 27.4 metres. Atlanta Magazine put it fairly in April 2025, calling it relatively small next to other trees and huge for its species. The program's record ranks it first among the city's black tupelos, while the magazine's list puts it second with a crown about 14 metres across, so its place depends on which list you read.

Levine's point was its staying power. It has been on the list for almost two decades, he said, and it still stands tall and has beautiful fall colours. Those colours are the reason to come in autumn.

This is a private home. The tree is clearly visible from the street, so look from the public sidewalk on Moreland Avenue NE and leave the garden to the people who live there.

Nobody has published its age. If you know when it was planted, tell us.
